title: Victim Selection (Predatory Targeting)
description: Predators do not attack randomly. They observe and select victims based on subtle signals of vulnerability.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Predators do not attack randomly. They observe and select victims based on subtle signals of vulnerability—posture, gait, distraction, or lack of environmental awareness—that mark a person as an easier target.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A mugger watches a crowd and picks the one person with slumped shoulders and downcast eyes.
A con artist notices someone who seems lonely or eager to please and strikes up a conversation.
A sexual predator approaches a woman who is walking slowly, head down, with a phone in hand, not scanning her surroundings.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Surveillance: watching the area for 5–15 minutes, ignoring most, focusing on a few.
Testing: a brief, low-stakes approach (asking for a light, a question) to gauge response and compliance.
Rehearsal: moving in and out of the target’s space to see if they notice or react.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “He’s too busy with his phone to see me coming.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Someone’s attention lingers on you longer than is normal.
Someone mirrors your path or changes direction to test your awareness.
A stranger asks an unnecessarily personal or prying question early.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Grayson & Stein (1981) found that prisoners could identify easy targets through shared traits: short stride, asymmetrical gait, slow movement, and lack of eye contact. Predators exploit predictable, unassertive body language.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Walk with a confident stride, head up, scanning your environment.
Do not let phones or headphones distract you in transitional spaces.
If approached with a “test” request, give a calm but non-compliant response: “Sorry, I can’t help.”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Believing clothing or attractiveness is the main factor; research shows movement and awareness matter more.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A woman walking home fumbles for keys while looking down, her free hand holding a phone. A man across the street observes her for three minutes, then crosses to follow. He bypasses a man who is walking briskly and scanning around. The woman never notices him until he’s too close.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Predators shop for victims who don’t look back. Your awareness is your first and loudest “no.”
